item.title: Welcome 2026
item.description:
Good reading start to 2026 - I’ve read a bunch of books in January!

  1. When things fall apart - Pema Chodron (great book, for mindfulness + meditation + Tibetan Buddhism)
  2. John & Paul: A Love Story in Songs - Ian Leslie (fantastic story, well written, a bit technical for me on the song structure, but great story anyway…)
  3. The Dalai Lama’s Book of Transformation - Dalai Lama (fantastic short book, worth re-reading multiple times)
  4. The Ramayana: RK Narayan’s translation (short translation, well written, skips some of the important stories, based on Kamban Ramayana)
  5. Inside Out: A Personal History of Pink Floyd - Nick Mason (funny, engaging, and super fun read, Nick Mason is a fun writer!)
  6. Why I am a Hindu - Sashi Tharooor (enjoyed the first part, skipped most of the middle of the book; learnt the differene between Secular, Syncretic, and Pluralist)

item.title: Mother Mary Comes to Me
item.description:
Brilliant memoir / biography by Arundhati Roy. She can write! Oh my God - wish I could write like that. Her portrait of her mother, Mary Roy, through a biographical recounting of her own life was superb. Took me back to Delhi in the 80’s and 90’s, a lot seemed similar, though much of her book was set in the ‘60’s and ‘70’s.

Ended up watching the brilliant “In Which Annie Gives It Those Ones” after reading the book.

item.title: 4 short books
item.description:
Read 4 short books:

  1. The sense of an ending, Julian Barnes: Good, but a bit grim, not to my taste
  2. Zorba the Greek: Very Good, and a lot of fun
  3. The Razors Edge, Somerset Maugham: Really really good, what writing!
  4. Essays after 80, Donald Hall: Fantastic essays

item.title: Lonesome Dove, McMurtry
item.description:
Read Lonesome Dove recommended to me by my friends Akshay & Shahana over the last few weeks… it’s a long book, adding to the list of long books I’ve read this year.

I enjoyed the book, but I can’t say I got much out of it - it’s a rambling story, a bit simple, that captures your attention and keeps you reading. I read most of it during my trip to LA & Phoenix, which made the book come to life more somehow, being set close to the Mexican border (at least to start!).

item.title: 2666, Roberto Bolano
item.description:
Read this for the most part during the trip to Sikkim. Read a lot of it in the car, on my Kindle.

2666 was weird. the writing style is simple and captivating, and so much is happening (funnnily, i thought about the various sub-stories and meanderings in the mahabharata). the book about the murders of the women was a gut-punch. the book was like a rogue river, it flowed whereever it wanted, senseless and yet singular. brilliant and headachy.

item.title: The Passion According to G.H, Clarice Lispector
item.description:
• Finished reading on 26/06/2025
  • Brilliant book, 5 stars, real gut-punch
  • Disgustingly good short book
  • Disturbing, awakening
  • Themes/Thoughts:
    • Living in the moment / action orientation, rather than “hope” which is hopeless and in the future
    • The Sacred in everything, even (and especially in the profane)
    • To not construct concepts through words (like ‘beauty’, etc.)
    • To reject sensitivity and sentimentality
    • To know what you need, and to fulfill it: To strive, to live
    • To not be heroic, and to take tiny steps
    • To be inhuman, beyond human, alive
    • To be “independed”
  • Some quotes
    • “Cast of this humanization”
    • “This obsession with the future”
    • “This obsession with naming things”
    • Organizing -> leading to not experiencing
    • Material world
    • The bordom / in-between is reality
  • Key concepts
    • The limits of langauge (speaking the unknowable)
    • The collapse of identity
    • The obsession with form and destruction
    • Sacred in the profane
    • Time and being
    • Death and resurrection
    • Asking v/s Being
  • Related to
    • Neitsche, Spinoza
    • Panentheism, Buddhism
    • Confucious and Dao resolution

item.title: The Glass Bead Game
item.description:
My quick jotting down / notes… and discussions with chatgpt!

few things stood out:

  1. age of feuilleton felt very relatable to what’s happening with memes and instagram etc. right now
  2. his friends - tegularius, designori, and his influences - jacobius, music master were written well.
  3. i could see some of myself in the characters themselves: my leaving microsoft and the conversations i had then with my mentors felt parallel to the last chapter, esp. because i left at the peak; i could also relate to tegularius (overly intellectual, not in the world) and to designori (worn down by the cares of the world, stopping meditation, drinking more)… it was fascinating…

Going back to the book, The Glass Bead Game, the book seems to be written by a fairly modest biographer. Is this ironic? It makes the book harder to read than, let’s say, Siddhartha by Hermann Hesse. So clearly Hermann Hesse is a brilliant writer, but was affecting the tone of a modest biographer.

item.title: A House for Mr. Biswas
item.description: My quick jotting down… “I completed reading A House for Mr. Biswas. It was really good. I really liked how the story was just constructed really beautifully with humor, pathos, disgust, sadness. It was a great humanist novel: struggling, struggling for more, despite circumstances that hold you back, wanting more, rebelling against custom, not knowing why and yet trying to find your own path. I could imagine it made into a great movie, by someone like Satyajit Ray… overall, I loved the book.”

item.title: On my TOREAD list for 2025
item.description:
Books on my TOREAD list for 2025

  1. 📘 Lonesome Dove – Larry McMurtry Epic Western of love, loss, and legacy. Heart-forward and unforgettable. (Reading before your birthday)

  2. 📕 Life and Fate – Vasily Grossman A war novel that wrestles with power, morality, and humanity on a massive scale. (Reading before your birthday)

  3. 📗 In Search of Lost Time – Marcel Proust A layered meditation on memory, identity, and the passing of time. (Reading from August to December)
